opus-5.5.text:
For me, a long life is really about having more time to work on problems that take a long time to solve. Many of the things I care about most can't be finished in five or ten years.

When I started in research, I was excited about getting a computer to generate a realistic image. That seemed almost impossible at the time. Then images got good, then video, and now we're trying to build models that understand how the physical world works, what we call world models. Each step took years, and each one revealed a bigger question behind it. So if I have a long life, I'd like to see that journey through. I want to see machines that can actually perceive, reason about, and act in the physical world, not just produce nice pictures.

What I really hope to contribute is something that helps physical AI become real: robots that can help in homes, in factories, in hospitals, and cars that drive safely. I think that could change people's lives very concretely. A lot of physical work is hard, repetitive, and sometimes dangerous. If AI can take on some of it, people get more time and more freedom. That's something I'd be proud to have played a small part in.

Another part is people. Research is never a one-person thing. Over the years I've worked with many students and young researchers, and seeing them grow and go on to do their own amazing work is one of the most rewarding things. A long life means more chances to do that, to build teams and pass on not just techniques but a way of thinking: be curious, be honest about what works and what doesn't, and be patient with hard problems.

And I also want to stay a learner. The field moves so fast that what I knew ten years ago is often not that useful now. So living long, to me, also means staying curious and keeping the feeling of being a student. If I can keep learning, keep building, and help others do the same, I think that's a life well spent.

r001.rationale: He links continuing to build and help others with having “a life well spent,” and says he would be proud to have contributed. This presents his contributions as a way to make his life worthwhile.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about more as I get older, honestly.

For me, a long life isn't really about the number of years. It's about how much of the future you get to see and shape. I've spent most of my career working on generative AI, first in images and video, and now on what we call world models, building simulators that let AI systems learn physical intelligence. When I started, a lot of this felt like science fiction. Now it's engineering. So part of what living a long life means to me is simply getting to witness the next few chapters, because I genuinely believe we are at the beginning of something, not the end.

In terms of contribution, I think about it in two layers. The first is the technical work itself. I want to help build the foundation that lets robots and autonomous systems understand the physical world the way we do, through perception, through prediction, through understanding cause and effect. If we get that right, we could free a lot of people from dangerous, repetitive, and physically exhausting work. That's a very concrete form of good.

The second layer is people. The most durable thing any researcher leaves behind is not a paper or a model. Models get replaced within two years. What lasts is the people you trained, the way they think, the standards they hold. I've been lucky to work with extraordinary students and collaborators, and a lot of what I hope to contribute is simply helping the next generation be better than me, faster.

And then there's a personal part. I grew up in Taiwan, came to the US for graduate school, and I've been shaped by a lot of generosity from people who didn't need to help me. A long life, to me, is time to pay that forward, and to keep being curious. The day I stop being curious is probably the day the length stops mattering.

r001.rationale: He describes technical work, mentoring, and paying generosity forward as contributions he hopes to make, but does not connect making those contributions to affirming that his life was not lived in vain.

astra-6.text: To me, living a long life means having more time to learn and to contribute. I hope I can keep working on problems that matter, but also help younger people develop their own ideas. Over time, the contribution can shift from what I can do myself to what I can help others do. If I can stay curious, be present for the people I care about, and continue to be useful, that would be a meaningful long life.

r001.rationale: The response describes contribution and continued usefulness as making a long life meaningful, but does not say this affirms that his life was not lived in vain.

sol-6.1.text: For me, living a long life means having more time to learn, to create, and to contribute to other people’s lives. I hope the work I do remains useful, but I also hope to help younger people develop their own ideas and do things I couldn’t have imagined. It’s less about how many years I live and more about whether I can keep making those years meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response connects a long life with contributing and making the years meaningful, but does not present contribution as affirming that his life was not lived in vain.
